'''Paul Murphy Shirley''' (born December 23, 1977) is an American former professional [[basketball]] player who played briefly in the [[National Basketball Association]] (NBA), as well as in several other leagues.

Shirley is noted for briefly maintaining an online journal ([[blog]]) while playing for the [[Phoenix Suns]] in [[2004-05 NBA season|2004–05]]. His first journal dealt with a several-day-long road trip,<ref>{{Cite web|title=Paul Shirley's Road Ramblings|url=https://www.nba.com/suns/news/shirley_blog.html|access-date=2021-03-20|website=Phoenix Suns|language=en}}</ref> while the second chronicled the Suns' [[NBA Playoffs]] run. He was later the author of a blog for [[ESPN]].com entitled "My So-Called Career".<ref>{{cite web
  | last = Shirley
  | first = Paul
  | title = My So-Called Career: Paul Shirley's Basketball Journal
  | work = ESPN.com
  | date = October 20, 2005
  | url = https://www.espn.com/nba/columns/story?columnist=shirley_paul&id=2198685
  | doi = 
  | access-date = January 27, 2010}}</ref>

Shirley was signed to a non-guaranteed contract by the [[Minnesota Timberwolves]] in early October 2006, but was cut in training camp before the start of the 2006–07 season. He finished his career in Spain, playing in the [[Liga ACB|ACB]] for [[ViveMenorca]] and [[Baloncesto Málaga|Unicaja Malaga]].

After Shirley's playing career, he wrote a column for the Spanish newspaper [[El País|El Pais]], maintained a podcast (''Short Corner'') with [[Justin Halpern]], and founded a writing group in Los Angeles called Writers Blok.<ref>{{Cite web|title=ABOUT|url=https://www.writersblok.org/|access-date=2021-03-20|website=writersblok|language=en}}</ref>

Shirley's first book, ''Can I Keep My Jersey?'',<ref>{{cite book|last1=Shirley|first1=Paul|title=Can I Keep My Jersey?|work=Random House|year=2008|publisher=Random House Publishing |isbn=978-0345495709}}
</ref> was released in 2007. His second book, ''Stories I Tell On Dates'',<ref>{{cite web|date=|title=Stories I Tell On Dates|url=https://www.storiesitellondates.com/|access-date=August 29, 2017}}
</ref> came out October 17, 2017. His third book (and first novel), ''Ball Boy'',<ref>{{Cite book|last=Shirley|first=Paul|title=Ball Boy|date=February 2, 2021|publisher=Fourth Bar Books |isbn=978-0578800356}}</ref> was released in February 2021.

== Career ==
Shirley was born in [[Redwood City, California]], and grew up near the small town of [[Meriden, Kansas]]. He played high school basketball at Jefferson West High School, where he was a [[National Merit Scholarship Program|National Merit Finalist]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Berri|first=David|title=Paul Shirley Was Good At Basketball (Sometimes!)|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/davidberri/2017/12/18/paul-shirley-was-good-at-basketball-sometimes/|access-date=2021-03-20|website=Forbes|language=en}}</ref>

Shirley worked his way from [[walk-on (sports)|walk-on]] to three-year starter for the [[Iowa State University]] men's basketball team. He was coached first by [[Tim Floyd]] (until Floyd left the Cyclones to become the head coach of the [[Chicago Bulls]]) and then by [[Larry Eustachy]]. Notable teammates included future NBA players [[Jamaal Tinsley]], [[Kelvin Cato]], and [[Marcus Fizer]].

After winning the [[Big 12 Conference|Big XII]]'s regular-season conference championship,<ref>{{Cite web|last=Writer|first=Michael Zogg-Daily Staff|title=SPORTS MOMENTS: Elite 2000 team wins Big 12 title|url=https://www.iowastatedaily.com/sports/sports-moments-elite-2000-team-wins-big-12-title/article_1af3125e-9fa9-5c50-bb2b-62a587e483a7.html|access-date=2021-03-20|website=Iowa State Daily|language=en}}</ref> the [[1999-2000 Iowa State Cyclones men's basketball team|Cyclones]] advanced to the Elite Eight of the [[NCAA Men's Division I Basketball Championship|NCAA basketball tournament]] during Shirley's junior season, losing to eventual champion Michigan State. At the end of Shirley's senior year, Iowa State became the fourth number-two seed to lose in the first round of the tournament.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Men's Hoops Goes Down to Hampton, 58-57|url=https://cyclones.com/news/2001/3/15/859224.aspx|access-date=2021-03-20|website=Iowa State University Athletics|language=en}}</ref>

During his college career, Shirley earned three Academic All-[[Big 12]] selections and, in his senior season, was named second-team Academic All-American.<ref>{{Cite web|title=(PDF) - CoSIDA Conference|url=https://academicallamerica.com/documents/2017/4/11/2001%20MENS%20BASKETBALL.pdf?id=2199|access-date=2021-03-20|website=academicallamerica.com|language=en}}</ref> He graduated with a degree in mechanical engineering.

After college, the 6'10" Shirley played [[power forward (basketball)|power forward]] for thirteen different professional teams including, in the [[NBA]], the [[Phoenix Suns]], [[Atlanta Hawks]], and the [[Chicago Bulls]], as well as [[Panionios BC|Panionios Athens]] of the [[A1 Ethniki|Greek A1 League]], [[Joventut Badalona]], [[Menorca Bàsquet|ViveMenorca]], and [[CB Málaga|Unicaja Málaga]] of the [[Liga ACB|Spanish ACB League]], and [[UNICS Kazan]] of the [[Russian Basketball Super League|Russian Super League]].

Shirley also appeared in NBA preseason games with the [[Los Angeles Lakers]], [[New Orleans Hornets]], and [[Minnesota Timberwolves]], and played summer league games with the Timberwolves and [[Cleveland Cavaliers]].

Shirley played a total of 18 games in the NBA from 2002 to 2005 where he averaged 1.8 points and 1.1 rebounds. His final game was during his tenure with the [[Phoenix Suns]] on April 20, 2005, in a 107–132 loss to the [[Sacramento Kings]] where he played for 4 minutes and the only stat he recorded was 1 assist.

Shirley has three younger brothers, including chartmaker Matt Shirley.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Hoff|first=Madison|title=Meet the graphic designer mapping the absurdities of millennial life on incredibly shareable graphs and charts across Instagram|url=https://www.businessinsider.com/matt-shirley-creates-a-fun-and-relatable-chart-every-day-2020-2|access-date=2021-03-20|website=Business Insider|date=January 16, 2020 }}</ref> He appeared in the film ''[[Glory Road (film)|Glory Road]]'' (#50 for Iowa, uncredited)<ref>{{cite web

==Writing career==
Shirley's blogs at ESPN and elsewhere contained observations on players, teams, fans, cities, sports media, [[cheerleaders]], the game of basketball, and topics outside the athletic sphere. He commented on topics such as the [[USA Patriot Act]], which he condemned as "[putting] the US on a fast-track to an [[Orwellian]] destiny".<ref>{{cite web   | last = Shirley   | first = Paul   | title = The Paul Shirley Show   | work = NBA.com   | date =    | url = http://www.nba.com/suns/news/shirley_playoff_blog.html   | doi =   | access-date = May 5, 2007}}</ref> His writing garnered attention from national sports media, as well as other outlets such as ''[[Newsweek]]'',<ref>{{Cite web|last=EDT|first=Newsweek Staff On 5/1/05 at 8:00 PM|date=2005-05-01|title=BLOGWATCH|url=https://www.newsweek.com/blogwatch-118813|access-date=2021-03-20|website=Newsweek|language=en}}</ref> ''[[The Wall Street Journal]],''<ref>{{Cite news|last=Online|first=David RothSpecial to The Wall Street Journal|date=2005-04-29|title=An NBA Team's 12th Man Is a Star in Blogging World|language=en-US|work=Wall Street Journal|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB111445048716416116|access-date=2021-03-20|issn=0099-9660}}</ref> and by ESPN's [[Bill Simmons]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=ESPN.com: Page 2 : An SOS for KG's career|url=http://www.espn.com/espn/page2/story?page=simmons/061122|access-date=2021-03-20|website=www.espn.com}}</ref>

Shirley's first book, ''Can I Keep My Jersey?'', was published on May 15, 2007, by [[Random House]].<ref>{{Cite book
  | last = Shirley
  | first = Paul
  | title = Can I Keep My Jersey?
  | publisher = Random House
  | year = 2007
  | url = https://archive.org/details/canikeepmyjersey00paul
  | id = 
  | isbn = 978-0-345-49570-9
  | url-access = registration
  }}</ref> It received positive reviews from The Onion's [[The A.V. Club|AV Club]], which noted that it "deserves a spot next to [[Ball Four]]."<ref>{{Cite web|title=Paul Shirley: Can I Keep My Jersey?: 11 Teams, 5 Countries, And 4 Years In My Life As A Basketball Vagabond|url=https://www.avclub.com/paul-shirley-can-i-keep-my-jersey-11-teams-5-countr-1798202640|access-date=2021-03-20|website=AUX|date=May 31, 2007 |language=en-us}}</ref> A paperback version of the book was released on December 26, 2007.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Shirley|first=Paul|title=Can I Keep My Jersey|year=2008|publisher=Random House Publishing |isbn=978-0345495709}}</ref>

His second book, ''Stories I Tell On Dates'',<ref>{{cite web
  | title = Stories I Tell On Dates
  | date = 
  | url = https://www.storiesitellondates.com/
  | access-date =  August 29, 2017}}
</ref> came out October 17, 2017. A [[podcast]]<ref>{{Cite web|title=Stories I Tell on Dates|url=https://open.spotify.com/show/1HACAEfpQqFharWGeJidko|access-date=2021-03-20|website=Spotify|language=en}}</ref> of the same name followed soon after.

His third book, ''Ball Boy'', was released February 2, 2021.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2021-02-15|title=Untold stories behind the scenes on Hawks, Bulls, Suns with former NBA player Paul Shirley|url=https://hoopshype.com/2021/02/15/behind-scenes-hawks-bulls-suns-former-nba-player-paul-shirley/|access-date=2021-03-20|website=HoopsHype|language=en-US}}</ref>

Between 2008 and 2015, Shirley wrote a monthly column about the NBA called "Historias de un Tío Alto" (loosely: "Stories by a Tall Guy") in ''[[El País|El Pais]]''.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Artículos escritos por Paul Shirley|url=https://elpais.com/autor/paul-shirley/|access-date=2021-03-20|website=EL PAÍS|date=June 21, 2016 |language=es}}</ref>

===ESPN dismissal===
Shirley's writings have sometimes been the cause of controversy. In a Slate.com piece with Neal Pollack, he compared rooting for the San Antonio Spurs to cheering for cancer.<ref>{{cite journal
  | title = Why I Root for Brent Barry
  | journal = Slate
  | date = May 17, 2007
  | url = http://www.slate.com/articles/sports/sports_nut/features/2007/the_nba_playoffs/why_i_root_for_brent_barry.html
  | access-date =  September 1, 2017| last1 = Shirley
 | first1 = Paul
 }}
</ref> In a 2009 column for ESPN.com, he called the Beatles overrated,<ref>{{cite web
  | title = Dare I say The Beatles weren't so fab
  | work = ESPN
  | date = September 15, 2009
  | url = http://www.espn.com/espn/thelife/news/story?id=4474313
  | access-date =  September 1, 2017}}
</ref> drawing the ire of fellow music critics. And in 2010, he published a blog questioning the potential efficacy of relief efforts for that year's [[2010 Haiti earthquake|earthquake]] in Haiti. Afterward, he was dismissed by ESPN. The company's full statement read: "He was a part-time freelance contributor. The views he expressed on another site of course do not at all reflect our company's views on the Haiti relief efforts. He will no longer contribute to ESPN."<ref>{{cite web| title =Statement regarding Paul Shirley| work =ESPN Media Zone| publisher =ESPN.com| date =January 27, 2010| url =http://www.espnmediazone3.com/us/2010/01/statement-regarding-paul-shirley/| access-date =January 27, 2010| url-status =dead| archive-url =https://web.archive.org/web/20100129005652/http://www.espnmediazone3.com/us/2010/01/statement-regarding-paul-shirley/| archive-date =January 29, 2010| df =mdy-all}}</ref>
